title: Object Pose & Embodied Perception
summary: Working out where an object is — for objects the system has never seen before.
description: Most pose estimators are trained on the objects they will later meet. We work on the case that actually occurs outside a lab: an object arrives with no CAD model, no category label and no training run of its own. Our methods recover full 6D pose from a handful of reference views, from a single RGB image, or from language alone — and they are built to survive what benchmarks usually leave out: specular and transparent surfaces, cluttered industrial bins, and objects that will not hold still. The group runs the TRICKY and category-level challenges at ICCV to put those failure cases in front of the whole field.

title: Neural Scene Representation & 4D Dynamics
summary: Scenes that are not just reconstructed but keep moving — geometry with time built in.
description: A reconstruction that freezes the world at one instant is of little use to a robot or a monitoring system. We build representations carrying time as a first-class dimension: neural ODEs that continue a scene's motion past the end of the observed sequence, Gaussian splats recovered from image pairs whose camera poses are unknown, radiance fields that stay stable while both the scene and the camera move. The recurring question is how much can be extrapolated from how little.

title: Robotic & Interventional Imaging
summary: Making ultrasound, endoscopy and X-ray legible to machines — and to the clinician holding the probe.
description: Medical imaging breaks the assumptions computer vision is built on: no texture to match, no reliable lighting, anatomy that deforms as it is observed, and almost no labelled data. We work on self-supervised segmentation and tracking that needs no annotation, implicit representations that compensate for breathing during a robotic sweep, common anatomical spaces that let CT and ultrasound be compared at all, and highlight removal that recovers the surface an endoscope is actually looking at.

title: Earth Observation & Small-Satellite Missions
summary: From mission design to the pixel — building the sensor as well as the algorithms that read it.
description: This group does not only process satellite imagery; it helps build the satellite. In CuBy — Satellite Network Bavaria we accompany a multispectral small-satellite mission for the State of Bavaria from mission design through payload evaluation, camera simulation, pre-launch calibration and on-orbit calibration strategy, all the way to the products at the far end: cloud masking, super-resolution, georeferencing. Aquila pushes the resolution question further, asking how much detail can be recovered from a microsatellite constellation without hallucinating any of it.

title: Digital Twins of the Built World & Forensics
summary: Reconstructions precise enough to be evidence, and legible enough to be questioned.
description: A digital twin is only worth building if you can ask it something. Working with the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office, we reconstruct scenes as geometrically accurate, photorealistic twins and then make them answerable — instance-level inventories of the objects present, open-vocabulary queries over them, and agents that reason about where those objects sit in relation to one another. The same methods documented human rights violations in Visual Investigations, shown at the Pinakothek der Moderne.

title: Aerial Robotics & Autonomous Perception
summary: Perception for aircraft that have to decide where to look, and where to land.
description: An autonomous aircraft needs an answer before it has all the data. With TUM's Institute of Flight System Dynamics we build the whole stack for landing-site detection in unstructured terrain — a synchronised LiDAR–RGB sensor rig, deployment in ROS2, multimodal fusion for robust aerial perception — and add language, so a site can be described rather than merely scored. A second line asks where to point the camera next: next-best-view planning that finds what a forest canopy is hiding.
